sections.html:
• Other names: Bruun's cleaner shrimp, False anemone shrimp, Clear cleaner shrimp, Floating shrimp, Red arrow cleaning shrimp, Rock shrimp, Spotted cleaner shrimp, Jelly cleaner shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: about 40 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore / carnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 3 years
  • Colour: transparent with tiny white and red dots

Urocaridella antonbruunii was initially described from the Comoro Islands. Today the species has a circum-tropical distribution throughout the Indo-West Pacific region, e.g. Kenya, Australia, New Caledonia, Japan, Hawaii, the Comoro Islands, Indonesia, the Great Barrier Reef, the Palau Islands, Dzaoudzi, Pamanzi Island, the Seychelles and the South China Sea.

The red-white cleaner shrimp is generally found in shallow tropical reef waters and crevices at 1–12 m depth. In some regions it has been observed deeper, for example 20 m in the Comoro Islands, 26 m in Indonesia and even 60 m in South China.

In the wild it is found free-living and on a wide array of substrates (rocky shorelines, hard-bottom reefs, tube sponges, etc.), suggesting that its transparent body is not particularly related to any habitat type. It inhabits shallow waters where the current is very slow-moving.

Because of their small size there are no strict minimum requirements. Even a 40-litre marine tank is good enough for a few red-white cleaner shrimp. A larger tank is better for the stability of water chemistry, but these small shrimp may get lost in large tanks unless kept in large numbers.

Urocaridella antonbruunii is a relatively hardy species. Keeping it in a marine tank is not complicated because it has no special water quality requirements. These shrimp should be kept under conditions suitable for any typical marine aquarium.

Most of them are wild-caught and are often delivered to pet stores in poor condition. Before putting them into the tank, at least temperature-acclimate them. Give them time to acclimatise and do not rush the process, as sudden changes can harm them.

• Temperature: 24–27 °C
  • pH: 8.0–8.4
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm is optimal, but it can be a bit lower or higher
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm

Avoid fast-moving water flow if possible: in the wild these shrimp live where the current is very slow, and strong surface agitation makes them uncomfortable and stressed.

Lighting: the shrimp do not really need light, so lighting can be adapted to the needs of the corals and fish in the tank.

Substrate: they are not diggers and have no preference for the substrate.

Decorations: decorations play an important role, providing hiding places (shelter and protection) and minimising stress. This is also crucial for moulting. In a community tank there should be plenty of dark areas to hide in, created from rocks, PVC pipe, plastic tunnels, fake plants, etc.

These marine shrimp are opportunistic omnivores with a strong preference for high-protein food (such as copepods and small microorganisms). In the wild they have a cleaning symbiotic relationship with fish, removing ectoparasites, mucus, scales or diseased tissue, which they eat as part of their diet.

They do best when fed sinking food and accept a wide range of fish, shrimp or sea anemone foods. No direct feeding is necessary. Any pellet, flake and gel foods that provide animal-based nutrition will work. Meaty food with higher fat content can accelerate growth, but risks water quality problems.

Do not treat red-white cleaner shrimp as simple scavengers that can survive on the leftovers from feeding community fish, or as aquarium janitors. If there is leftover food in the tank, the tank is being overfed; the solution is to feed less.

Foods they enjoy:

  • Artemia,
  • copepods,
  • mussel,
  • mysis shrimp,
  • plankton,
  • flake food,
  • thức ăn đông lạnh,
  • small pieces of fish or shrimp.

Urocaridella antonbruunii is not aggressive and can coexist peacefully with other inhabitants. It is completely harmless in the community tank.

Like most shrimp, it is very social and tends to gather in large groups, potentially reflecting its small size and limited defensive capability. The bigger the colony, the safer the shrimp feel and the more confident they act, venturing out of hiding more often. They are shy and skittish, especially in small groups, and do not like to be touched or handled.

It is known as a cleaner shrimp because it feeds on external parasites of fish, although it is not as effective as, for example, Lysmata amboinensis.

These shrimp swim a lot. Their pleopods (swimming legs) are strong enough to let them remain motionless in open water, and while swimming the walking legs hang loosely under the abdomen.

According to studies, in the wild they are active both by day and by night. In aquariums they are mostly nocturnal, with activity starting at sunset and gradually stopping before sunrise. This is normal behaviour, mainly associated in nature with avoiding visual predators while feeding.

  • Social: yes
  • Active: at night
  • Peaceful: yes

Reef safe: generally yes. They should not cause problems in reef tanks and will not harm corals if they are not starving.

Tankmates: the ideal is a species tank, but they can be kept with other fish if chosen with care. Avoid aggressive eaters and large predators (such as triggerfish, wrasses, hawkfish, angelfish, etc.). They get along well with their own kind, so keeping a group is not a problem. They can also coexist peacefully with some other shrimp (for example peppermint shrimp, Lysmata debelius, Lysmata amboinensis, saron shrimp, bumblebee shrimp) and snails (cerith snails, bumblebee snails, conch snails, nassarius snails, etc.). Do not keep them with most crabs (for example Sally Lightfoot crab, arrow crab, emerald crab) or aggressive shrimp species (coral banded shrimp, harlequin shrimp, etc.).

• The larger shrimp are all females. Males are smaller.
  • Because females carry eggs, the underside (abdomen) of the female is wider and curves downward to protect the eggs. Males are thinner.
  • Females have longer pleopods since they carry eggs.
  • The presence of the saddle or eggs; because of the transparent body, the saddle is very easy to see.
  • The presence or absence of an appendix masculina on the second pleopods.

It is possible, although very difficult, to breed Urocaridella antonbruunii in a home aquarium. So far there have been only a few reports of successful breeding, so the trade is entirely based on wild-caught animals. Little is known about the larval, postlarval and juvenile stages.

Mating: the life cycle starts with mating, a very brief process (a few seconds). Females moult before mating and release a chemical substance into the water to attract males, signalling that the female is ready to spawn. The shrimp become mature when the carapace is around 5.2 mm.

Ovarian maturation generally takes place if a mated pair is kept under stable conditions. Maturation diets have been shown to affect fecundity and offspring quality. Common practice in shrimp culture is to use fresh frozen foods supplemented with artificial diets. Such items include squid, mussels, polychaetes and Artemia biomass, with artificial diets used only as a supplement.

Eggs: the average number of larvae per batch is around 123 ± 23. Fecundity increases with the body length of the female.

Hatching: larvae are generally produced after 5 to 6 weeks. It is important to provide adequate food to larvae immediately after hatching to avoid the effects of early starvation. The main problem of commercial culture of ornamental shrimp is the long larval development and poor survival rates.

Urocaridella antonbruunii was described by marine biologist Alexander James Bruce in 1967. The species is named in honour of Dr. Anton Frederik Bruun for his outstanding contribution to international oceanography. The genus name Urocaridella derives from the Greek 'oura' meaning 'tail' and the Latin 'carid' meaning marine 'crustacean'.

The species is similar in general appearance to shrimp of the genus Ancylomenes, both in its transparent body and colour pattern. However, unlike those shrimp, it is not associated with sea anemones, hence the name False anemone shrimp. It is morphologically closest to Urocaridella urocaridella, Urocaridella cyrtorhyncha, Urocaridella pulchella and Urocaridella arabianensis. To distinguish these species, scientists mostly compare the ratio of the rostrum and carapace, the length of the fingers and carpus of the pereiopods, the presence or absence of a mandible palp, and the structure of the 3rd abdominal posterodorsal region, not only colour patterns.

Description: a small saltwater shrimp reaching a maximum of about 3.5–4 cm in the aquarium (generally even a little less than 3 cm).

  • The slender, transparent body has scattered tiny white and red spots over the carapace and abdomen. Because of the translucent body, the stomach, digestive gland and ovary (orange or light green depending on the development of vitellogenesis) are easy to see.
  • A very long white-red rostrum angled upwards, with red and white patches at the tip.
  • A distinctive hump on the body. The hump of the third abdominal somite bears two red bars and a white line (often intermittent).
  • Red and white bands occur throughout the first and second walking legs (pereiopods). The first pair of claws is smaller than the second. The last three walking legs have red and white bands with red and white spots on the basal segments.
  • The eyes are translucent, stalked, large and prominent.
  • Long red antennae and antennules with a few white dots at the base.
  • The walking legs are long, slender and semi-transparent with white and red bands.
  • The pleopods (swimmerets) are almost transparent with red and white spots on the basipod.
  • At the base of the telson there may be a red or white band, followed by 2 or 3 large white dots.

Small shrimp are less pigmented than large ones.

Lifespan: there is no data on the maximum lifespan in the wild. In captivity, with appropriate care, they can reproduce and live up to 2–3 years.
